cues.text: A Doubt at the Breaking of the Bread
On April 25, 1356, an unnamed priest was celebrating Mass in the chapel of the Church of St. Catherine in Macerata .
The chapel was owned by Benedictine monks.
In the moments before Communion, he found himself struck by doubt over the Real Presence of Christ in the consecrated Host he was about to break.
At the precise moment he broke the Host, tradition holds, an abundance of blood flowed out from it, staining part of the corporal beneath.
It also stained the chalice placed on the altar—a sign so immediate and directly tied to his own private doubt that the priest reported it at once, rather than attempt to conceal or explain it away.
The priest informed Bishop Nicholas of San Martino without delay.
The bishop ordered the blood-stained relic carried to the cathedral and opened a formal canonical process to examine the matter.
The sixteenth-century historian Ferdinando Ughelli would later cite this response in his own account of the episode.
One of the first confraternities dedicated to the Blessed Sacrament in Macerata was established in 1494, drawing directly on devotion to this relic.
The practice of the Forty Hours' adoration was introduced to the city in 1556— institutional fruits of a single Mass's private doubt over a century and a half earlier.
The stained corporal remains venerated today beneath the altar of the Most Holy Sacrament in the Cathedral of Macerata.
It rests alongside the original parchment describing the event and is still carried in solemn procession through the city each year on the feast of Corpus Christi.
The bloodstains, faded but visible, remain legible nearly seven centuries after a priest's plain confession of doubt was met, in the memory the Church has kept, with a sign rather than a rebuke.
